newsitem.title: DENMARK: Nordic ministers seek to halt bikers' war.
newsitem.headline: Nordic ministers seek to halt bikers' war.

text.p: Nordic justice ministers decided on Friday to take joint action to halt a bikers' war in which rival gangs armed with heavy weapons have killed and maimed one another across the region.

The ministers from Finland, Norway, Sweden and Denmark agreed at a council of war in Copenahgen to pool intelligence between national police forces more intensively and open a joint register of stolen weapons.
A joint statement said the four would consult on pending legislation and coordinate input to a Danish-led biker crime unit set up at the European police agency Europol in The Hague.
A Nordic working group to harmonise laws relating to biker crime would hold its first meeting in Finland next Thursday, Danish Justice Minister Bjoern Westh told a news conference.
A move that Norway's Grete Faremo said could be among the most important would be a joint effort, involving police, tax and excise officials, to trace the gangs' sources of income.

Danish police have long said that the bikers' expensive Harley Davidson motorcycles, frequent foreign travel, comfortable clubhouses, gold chains and lavish use of drink and drugs indicate wealth far beyond their visible incomes.

The Hell's Angels and Bandidos gangs have been fighting each other across the Nordic region for almost three years, with knives, pistols and chains giving way to stolen army machine guns, hand grenades and anti-tank missiles.
Seven people have been killed, others have had their legs blown off or their flesh mangled by grenade fragments and automatic weapons fire since the war went into high gear in February 1994.
Investigators say individual gang members deal in drugs, prostitutes and extortion but they have so far been unable to prove organised group involvement.

"There is no doubt that the most important motive in biker crime is money," Faremo told reporters after the 90-minute meeting. Like Denmark, she said, Norway was considering reversing the burden of proof in certain cases.

"It would be those criminals convicted of serious crime who would have to prove that they have earned their fortunes legally. That would be of course to turn things around and we would have to be very careful to protect the rights of the individual in such a measure," she said.
The ministers said they would ask their national police chiefs to meet soon to discuss concrete joint measures.
Denmark's parliament passed a rush bill on Thursday aimed at discouraging bikers from using heavily-fortified clubhouses in densely-populated residential areas.
Neighbours of attack-prone gang clubhouses fear that sooner or later they or their children will fall in the crossfire of the gang war.
The new Danish legislation would allow police to bar named persons from entering specific buildings where there was reason to believe that their presence could endanger others in the neighbourhood.
Westh said this was only a prelude to a package of legislation he hoped to bring to parliament in November, granting police much broader gang-busting powers.
"This law is is first and foremost to reduce the danger to neighbours, not to smash the gangs. That will follow," he said.
